title: Scaling with parallelism
hypothesis: Doubling the cores available to Spark gives at least 1.6 times speed-up.
conclusion: local[1]: 54.5s wall clock, 53.7s of work after removing 0.8s of fixed cost; local[2]: 33.7s wall clock, 33.0s of work after removing 0.7s of fixed cost; local[4]: 39.7s wall clock, 39.2s of work after removing 0.6s of fixed cost. Speed-up on the work component against one core: local[1] 1.0x, local[2] 1.628x, local[4] 1.37x. Doubling from 2 to 4 cores gave 0.842x, against the hypothesis's 1.6x threshold: not met.. Core utilisation (executor run time over wall clock x cores): local[1] 0.646, local[2] 0.671, local[4] 0.678; shuffle written: local[1] 21354713 bytes, local[2] 22436948 bytes, local[4] 24357717 bytes; spill: local[1] 0 bytes, local[2] 0 bytes, local[4] 0 bytes. Sub-linear scaling is the expected observation; the window aggregations shuffle, and shuffling does not halve when the cores double. This is intra-node scaling inside one JVM, not distributed workers, and the 100 GB tier was not run - see the limitations.
limitations: The 100 GB tier was not run and is not estimated: Docker has a 5.27 GB VM here (ADR-0002).

Distributed workers were not used. Compose can start a Spark master and one worker, but with 8 host cores and ~3 GB usable for containers two workers would contend for the same cores and the result would measure scheduling overhead, not scaling. `local[N]` varies the same knob - cores available to the work - inside one JVM, so there is no network shuffle and no cross-machine spill. The numbers below describe intra-node scaling only.
